newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Recovering Yeltsin urges unity, opponents march.
newsitem.headline: Recovering Yeltsin urges unity, opponents march.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin launched himself back into politics on Thursday just two days after open heart surgery, calling for national reconciliation as communist opponents marked the anniversary of the Russian revolution.

The 65-year-old leader continued to surprise doctors with his quick recovery from a quintuple heart bypass operation as thousands of communists took to the streets in cities across the country to mark the 79th anniversary of the 1917 Bolshevik coup.

Yeltsin hopes the heart surgery will not only save him from a lingering death but inject new life into his presidency -- he won a new four-year term in July -- and let him to push on with the reforms Russia needs after the collapse of the Soviet Union.
Renat Akchurin, the Russian surgeon who led the seven-hour operation on Tuesday, said the post-operative schedule had had to be adapted slightly because of Yeltsin's rapid progress.

"The president is recovering more quickly...he has somewhat altered our timetable, he got on his feet earlier...walked around his bed...met friends and family," he said in an interview on NTV television's "Hero of the Day" programme.

Issuing decrees from his hospital room, Yeltsin said he wanted to break with Russia's past of internal conflict and renamed the November 7 Revolution Day holiday. It will now be known as the Day of Accord and Reconciliation.
"The revolution of 1917 dramatically changed the destiny of our country," Yeltsin said in the decree, referring to the uprising which ushered in seven decades of communist rule.
"Keen not to allow confrontation in the future, in the interests of unity...I declare the November 7 holiday to be the Day of Accord and Reconciliation."
In a later appeal, he called for unity and reassured people he had returned to work.
"We are one nation. We have one fate, one future. And we are all from the same past."
He said the revolution saw hopes turn to tragedy.
"Society split apart. To this day, the nation is split into reds and whites, into us and them," he said. "It is time to end this. We have one Russia and we must be together."

But when Yeltsin leaves the Cardiology Research Centre in a western suburb of Moscow -- doctors advised him to stay another 24 hours -- he will face a restive population fed up with unpaid wages and pensions and fearful of a future bare of the comforting sausage-and-vodka certainties of the Soviet past.

Akchurin said Yeltsin could handle the bulk of his duties in 10 to 12 days. In the meantime, the president wants to be transferred to the more comfortable Central Clinical Hospital nearby, where he was treated for two heart attacks last year.
Revolution Day was the main annual Soviet holiday but has been shorn of the pomp of military parades through Red Square.
Yet demonstrators all over Russia used the day to revel in nostalgia for the past and protest about the present.
To the strains of the Internationale and the old Soviet national anthem, mostly elderly crowds trudged past the luxury hotels and shops that have sprung up in Moscow since 1991.

Yeltsin's appeal failed to convince Communist leader Gennady Zyuganov, who harangued the president before the Revolution Day faithful as they marched under portraits of Vladimir Lenin, founder of the Soviet state.
Zyuganov, who lost to Yeltsin in this year's presidential elections, said Russia was "on the edge of a precipice".
"There are two possibilities -- either total chaos leading to the next dictatorship and bloody struggle, or labour must unite...to establish a normal life," he told the crowd.
In a later statement, he refused to fall in with Yeltsin's appeal for unity.
"National peace and harmony are not decreed, they are achieved by intelligent, clever and tactical steps," he said.
But if the continuing barrage of optimistic medical bulletins issued by the Kremlin is to be believed, Yeltsin's political foes will find their sparring partner reinvigorated.
Pioneering U.S. heart surgeon Michael DeBakey, who was a consultant at the operation, said Yeltsin could be back at home in two to three weeks.
Russians would see a "vigorous leader" but it would be several weeks before he would be able to work at full strength.
